Neonatal Vipera berus emerge from the parchment-shelled egg after an incubation period that varies with maternal basking behavior, typically measuring 17 centimeters [Lb = 17 centimeters] in total length at hatching. This modest size at eclosion places the newly emerged hatchling within the expected range for a northern viperid, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the yolk-dependent embryo stage. The yolk-sac larva undergoes a brief endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which the juvenile must secure its first prey capture to sustain growth. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is generally reported as 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic mass for this species and corresponds to the maximum recorded body mass in adults across much of its European range.

Under controlled conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Vipera berus is realized through litters of 3 to 20 offspring [N_R_i = litters of 3 to 20 offspring] produced every other year [F_R_i =  every other year], with the majority of litters from 1969 onward containing between 10 and 14 neonates. This conservative reproductive strategy reflects the substantial energetic investment required during gestation in this viviparous viper, as gravid individuals must allocate considerable resources to support embryonic development over several months. Historical reports from Central European populations suggest that litter sizes rarely exceed the recorded maximum, with the most frequent counts clustering toward the lower end of the spectrum, a pattern that aligns with the energetic constraints of a cool-temperate climate.

The ultimate total length of Vipera berus is typically given as 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], although exceptionally large individuals may rarely attain 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] in total body length. This measurement, corresponding to the asymptotic length of the species, places the common European adder among the smaller-bodied members of the genus Vipera, with males generally remaining more modest in size than conspecific females. The rarely observed maximum of 90 centimeters likely represents the upper physiological limit achievable under optimal foraging conditions and minimal predation pressure, a size that has been sporadically recorded in long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Baltic region. Body length in this species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with adult females surpassing males in both mean and maximum snout-vent length, a pattern consistent with the selective pressures imposed by the need to accommodate developing offspring. Regional variation in ultimate length has been documented across the species' extensive Palearctic distribution.

When maintained at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], captive Vipera berus initiate their first reproductive event after approximately 1,278 days after birth [tR = approximately 1,278 days after birth], a timeline that reflects the species' relatively slow life history. This characteristic, common among temperate-zone vipers, requires several active seasons to accumulate sufficient body reserves before reproduction becomes energetically feasible. The first successful copulation typically occurs during the spring following the attainment of a minimum body size threshold, with vitellogenesis commencing shortly thereafter. Field studies from the Swiss Jura mountains corroborate this age estimate, indicating that most females begin breeding sometime during their fourth or fifth year of life, a delay that underscores the trade-off between somatic growth and early reproductive investment. The onset of gonadal activity in males appears to occur somewhat earlier, though reliable census data remain scarce.

Under the same laboratory conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for Vipera berus is approximately 7,300 days [am = approximately 7,300 days], representing over two decades of sustained physiological function in the absence of predation or disease. This longevity, measured as 20 years [am = 20 years] when converted to annual terms, is among the highest documented for a European viper and reflects the species' remarkably low extrinsic mortality rate in protected captive environments at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. In wild populations, senescence becomes apparent during the latter portion of this span, with older individuals exhibiting reduced foraging efficiency and a progressive deterioration of organ function that ultimately leads to natural mortality. The extended lifespan of Vipera berus is consistent with its iteroparous reproductive schedule and its position as a relatively slow-living predator within northern ecosystems, a life-history syndrome shared with other long-lived, viviparous reptiles. The oldest confirmed free-living individuals rarely exceed 15 years, indicating that field mortality truncates the potential longevity considerably.
